scenes.visual: Deep slate (#0F172A) schematic cell carried directly from the first film, showing the amber-gold (#F59E0B) membrane switch already jammed ON with a pulsing signal beam moving inward toward a coral-red (#F43F5E) safety gate. Title 'Many Mutations, One Weak Point' fades cleanly across the upper center, then clears.

scenes.tts: In the first film, one altered gene copy jammed a growth switch on. Why does one stuck switch rarely make a tumour? And why can blocking just one switch shrink a tumour with many mutations? Let us zoom out from that switch and watch the whole cell.
scenes.caption: In the first film, one altered gene copy jammed a growth switch on. Why does one stuck switch rarely make a tumour? And why can blocking just one switch shrink a tumour with many mutations? Let us zoom out from that switch and watch the whole cell.
scenes.visual: Camera pulls smoothly back from the jammed amber-gold (#F59E0B) switch and its two-copy chromosome rack to reveal the whole schematic cell: a glowing nucleus at center with a coral-red (#F43F5E) checkpoint barrier standing between the stuck amber signal and cell division.
scenes.narration: In the first film, one altered gene copy jammed a growth switch on. Why does one stuck switch rarely make a tumour? And why can blocking just one switch shrink a tumour with many mutations? Let us zoom out from that switch and watch the whole cell.

scenes.tts: You might expect a stuck growth switch to make a normal cell divide nonstop. Surprisingly, the cell usually stops instead. A healthy cell reads a nonstop growth signal as a dangerous fault, not a normal order. Internal safety guards called checkpoints catch the fault before the cell runs away.

scenes.visual: A brief normal amber pulse passes cleanly through the gate, then turns into a continuous, buzzing amber-gold (#F59E0B) beam from the jammed switch. Immediately, coral-red (#F43F5E) warning rings pulse outward from the barrier labelled 'Checkpoint (schematic)', clamping down across the division arrow so the cell stays single.

scenes.tts: One major guard is the checkpoint protein p fifty three. A nonstop growth signal alarms it much like damaged D N A does. It halts cell division at once or triggers apoptosis, which is programmed cell death. Even cells that slip past it still need survival signals to stay alive.
scenes.caption: One major guard is the checkpoint protein p53. A nonstop growth signal alarms it much like damaged DNA does. It halts cell division at once or triggers apoptosis, which is programmed cell death. Even cells that slip past it still need survival signals to stay alive.
scenes.visual: The coral-red (#F43F5E) barrier opens to highlight a bright coral-red badge labelled 'p53'. Two animated branches appear from p53: one locks the cell-cycle ring still ('Arrest'), and the other fades the schematic cell into fragments ('Apoptosis'). A faint emerald-teal (#10B981) survival cue beside the cell shows the survival requirement.
scenes.narration: One major guard is the checkpoint protein p53. A nonstop growth signal alarms it much like damaged DNA does. It halts cell division at once or triggers apoptosis, which is programmed cell death. Even cells that slip past it still need survival signals to stay alive.

scenes.tts: That is why one stuck switch is seldom enough for cancer. To become a tumour, a cell usually collects several cooperating changes over time. It may pair a stuck on-switch with a lost off-switch, a broken checkpoint, and blocked cell death. Step by step, those combined faults let a tumour grow.

scenes.visual: On the carried cell, fault badges snap on one by one in sequence (labelled 'Schematic'): amber-gold (#F59E0B) 'Stuck on-switch', dashed grey (#64748B) with crimson X (#EF4444) 'Lost off-switch', fractured coral-red (#F43F5E) 'p53 lost', and blocked apoptosis gate. With those changes combined, the single cell divides smoothly into a pulsing cluster of schematic tumour cells carrying all four badges.
scenes.narration: That is why one stuck switch is seldom enough for cancer. To become a tumour, a cell usually collects several cooperating changes over time. It may pair a stuck on-switch with a lost off-switch, a broken checkpoint, and blocked cell death. Step by step, those combined faults let a tumour grow.

scenes.tts: Now picture a tumour that already carries all of those mutations. Its checkpoint is gone, its off-switch is missing, and one growth switch is jammed on. Suppose a targeted drug shuts off only that one stuck switch, leaving every other mutation untouched. Will the tumour keep growing, or will it shrink?
scenes.caption: Now picture a tumour that already carries all of those mutations. Its checkpoint is gone, its off-switch is missing, and one growth switch is jammed on. Suppose a targeted drug shuts off only that one stuck switch, leaving every other mutation untouched. Will the tumour keep growing, or will it shrink?
scenes.visual: The schematic tumour cluster fills the center of the frame, with all its mutation badges clearly visible. A crisp cyan (#38BDF8) wedge labelled 'Targeted drug' glides in and fits cleanly into the amber-gold (#F59E0B) switch only; the amber glow turns off while the broken checkpoint and missing off-switch badges remain untouched. Question banner appears at top: 'Block only one stuck switch: keep growing or shrink?'
scenes.narration: Now picture a tumour that already carries all of those mutations. Its checkpoint is gone, its off-switch is missing, and one growth switch is jammed on. Suppose a targeted drug shuts off only that one stuck switch, leaving every other mutation untouched. Will the tumour keep growing, or will it shrink?

scenes.visual: The question 'Block only one stuck switch: keep growing or shrink?' remains clear at the top. The cyan (#38BDF8) drug sits locked inside the silenced switch while the other broken badges (dashed grey off-switch, fractured coral-red checkpoint) pulse gently on the schematic tumour cluster. A smooth progress bar runs across the bottom edge for 4.5 seconds.

scenes.tts: Often, the tumour shrinks, because its cells have come to lean on that one signal. Their other mutations stay untouched inside every cell, yet the cells stop dividing or die. Scientists call this dependence oncogene addiction. That is why one targeted drug can sometimes shrink a tumour carrying many mutations.

scenes.visual: The question fades out. With the cyan (#38BDF8) blocker holding the amber-gold switch dark, the schematic tumour cluster visibly stops pulsing and contracts as outer cells fade away, even though the other broken badges remain visible inside them. Label 'Oncogene addiction' appears cleanly beside the shrinking cluster.
scenes.narration: Often, the tumour shrinks, because its cells have come to lean on that one signal. Their other mutations stay untouched inside every cell, yet the cells stop dividing or die. Scientists call this dependence oncogene addiction. That is why one targeted drug can sometimes shrink a tumour carrying many mutations.

scenes.tts: Why does turning off one switch hit so hard? The exact cause is still debated, and two ideas lead. First, a stuck pathway keeps feedback brakes high, which may quiet nearby backup routes. Second, once the signal stops, survival signals may fade faster than death signals. Either way, the cell tips toward death.

scenes.visual: Two side-by-side schematic panels appear below the header 'Debated mechanisms (schematic)': left panel shows the loud amber-gold (#F59E0B) switch holding a feedback bar high that dims a parallel cool slate-blue (#60A5FA) backup route; right panel shows two decaying schematic curves after the cyan drug arrives—an emerald-teal (#10B981) 'Survival' curve dropping quickly while a coral-red (#F43F5E) 'Death' curve stays high longer, tipping a balance toward death.

First, a stuck pathway keeps feedback brakes high, which may quiet nearby backup routes. Second, once the signal stops, survival signals may fade faster than death signals. Either way, the cell tips toward death.

scenes.tts: Normal checkpoints guard a cell against a single jammed switch, so cancer usually requires several cooperating changes. Yet a tumour built around one loud driver can stay hooked on that single signal. Put both halves together clearly: tumours usually need several changes, yet often depend on one stuck switch.
